identity: A football terrace chant / crowd song about Van Dijk ('Van Dijk's knockout blow'), followed by long chanted runs of 'la la la...' and a refrain 'day day day / day al-shuja' (Dai the brave). Pure chant lyrics, laid out one chanted line per printed line.
law: LINE-DENSITY LAW (my doctrine 0g/0g-bis): 47 tokens over 10 printed lines, mean ~4 real tokens per line. This is the shortest-line regime there is. The printed line IS the unit. Cut at the <NL> line ends and NOWHERE inside a line. This is the same regime as doc_0696314023ab (the Batman title song), where I took 6 false cuts by firing PASS-2 clause laws inside verse lines and lost 20 F1. Verse/chant never reaches PASS 2.
reasoning: Site 1 - the repeated runs of 'la'. Eight, nine, ten identical tokens in a row with no connective is a textbook trigger for I4 (N parallel siblings with no connective = a list, cut before each) and for J1 (word drill, one word = one unit). BOTH ARE WRONG HERE and I am refusing them deliberately. I4/J1 apply to EXCHANGEABLE items - MCQ options, drill targets - things that stand alone as separate answers. A chanted 'la la la la' is not a list of eight items; it is ONE prolonged cry, a single sustained vocalisation. Nothing is exchangeable, nothing stands alone. Merging each run into its line is the only reading. Site 2 - line 1 'darbat Van Dijk al-qadiya' is a single noun phrase (a genitive construction plus adjective), not even two predications; no candidate at all. Site 3 - 'day day day' and 'day al-shuja': repetition-with-naming, the same family as F5 appositive escalation (nihaya haqiqiyya nihayat al-alam = ONE unit). Bare NPs with no verb, so by F7's discriminator (a verb is the line between apposition and enumeration) they merge. Site 4 - could two adjacent short lines MERGE across an <NL>? No: 0g explicitly says the line law never licenses merging across <NL>, and the format guarantees the token before every <NL> carries a boundary. Verdict: zero internal cuts; the answer is exactly the ten printed lines.
